title: Nikole Hannah-Jones ignores who failed her daughter — the teachers union teachers-union/
author: Daniel Di Martino
summary: Manhattan Institute fellow Daniel Di Martino argues that the failures Nikole Hannah-Jones describes at P.S. 307, including absent teachers, ungraded work, and an unadministered reading assessment, were the product of incentives rather than underfunding or segregation. He notes that the school spends over $50,000 per student with a nine-to-one student-teacher ratio and well-paid teachers, yet barely a quarter of students reach proficiency and fewer than half attend regularly. Every failure she catalogs, he argues, would get an employee fired in a private business, but tenure and a union contract make removal nearly impossible. His counterexample is Community Roots Charter School, less than a mile away, which serves similar students at roughly half the cost with proficiency above 80 percent. He concludes that Brooklyn's Black and Hispanic children need accountable adults rather than another lecture about segregation.
points: P.S. 307 spends over $50,000 per student per year, comparable to elite private school tuition.
Fewer than half of P.S. 307 students attend at least 90 percent of the time.
New York City teachers earn tenure after four years, after which removal requires lengthy just-cause hearings.
Community Roots Charter School posts proficiency above 80 percent and 91 percent regular attendance at about half the per-pupil cost.
New York's cap on charter schools limits how many families can access that alternative.
quotes: She’s seen firsthand how New York’s public school system exists to employ teachers — and educating students is an afterthought.
It’s not for lack of resources: P.S. 307 spends over $50,000 per student, per year, an amount equivalent to private school tuition in some of the best institutions in the country.

Every failure Hannah-Jones catalogs, whether absent teachers, ungraded work, faked assessments or no-show principals, is exactly the kind of failure that would get an employee fired in any private business.
Ratings, evaluations and discipline are all governed by a contract negotiated by the teachers’ union, whose entire purpose is to make sure no one is fired no matter what.
That means its teachers can be dismissed for not doing their jobs, its students can be expelled more easily for bad behavior that disrupts the class, and its parents have choices.
They need what Najya never got at P.S. 307: Administrators and teachers that are accountable for their students’ success.
